title: Short Stuff: Camberley Kate
summary: Short Stuff episode on Kate Ward, the 'Crazy Dog Lady' of Camberley, Surrey, England, who took in stray and abandoned dogs (and cats) starting in the 1940s with a lame greyhound from a vet, eventually caring for hundreds of animals at once. The hosts cover how she sourced animals from police stations and vets, her cart and street walks, her care and health of the dogs with help from vet Jeffrey Craddock, her clashes with the local council over a leash law, her letters to King George VI and Queen Elizabeth, her personality, her modest pension-based life, her legacy as a forerunner of modern rescue, and her death around 1979.

segments.title: Opening
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode about Camberley Kate, a figure they describe as a boss.

segments.title: The crazy dog lady of Camberley
segments.summary: Description of Kate Ward walking a large group of rescued dogs with a handmade cart through Camberley, Surrey, in the 1970s, and how she took in strays rather than fostering them.

segments.title: Origins with the greyhound Primo
segments.summary: Kate began her rescue work around 1943 after buying a cottage and rescuing a lame greyhound, Primo, from a vet who was about to put him down. The hosts note reports of hundreds of cats as well, and that she sourced animals from police stations and vets.

segments.title: Growth of the rescue and the BBC interview
segments.summary: Primo lived with her for many years. The hosts describe a mid-1970s BBC interview where her count of animals grew to about 500, then about 600 a few years later.

segments.title: Care for the dogs and remembering their names
segments.summary: The hosts clarify she was not running a farm-to-table operation. She cared for dogs well, could name each dog she had kept, and was 80 in an interview where she recalled them.

segments.title: Vet care, health of the dogs, and the leash law fight
segments.summary: Vet Jeffrey Craddock provided pro bono care and said her dogs were unusually healthy, living about sixteen years on average. Kate fought a leash law and was combative with cars and city council, and she also petitioned the royal family.

segments.title: Lion and the Unicorn and her personality
segments.summary: Kate was mentioned in Arthur Bryant's book The Lion and the Unicorn, which gave her a nickname. She was vocal and defensive about her dogs.

segments.title: Letters to King George VI and Queen Elizabeth
segments.summary: Kate wrote to King George VI after a teacher alleged she beat a dog, denying it. She also sent a wedding gift in 1947 to Princess Elizabeth, with a dog leash for the corgis.

segments.title: Modest life, early years, and legacy
segments.summary: Kate lived on a government pension, had been a housemaid, and was orphaned young. She bought her house for 600 pounds. The hosts describe her as a forerunner of modern dog rescue, with a Facebook page by Heather Driskgold Woodford documenting her.

segments.title: Death and tribute
segments.summary: Kate died around 1979, about age 84 by the hosts' estimate, after a series of strokes. The hosts salute her.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Short Stuff sign-off and iHeartRadio production credit.
